MODULE 42.1: DIVIDENDS, STOCK SPLITS, AND
SHARE REPURCHASES
LOS 42.a: Describe features and uses of dividends, share repurchases, stock
splits, and reverse stock splits.
Cash dividends, as the name implies, are payments made to shareholders in
cash, and they are subject to income tax in the period in which the cash flow is
received. Payment of dividends is discretionary and decided by a company’s
board of directors. Mature companies with relatively few growth opportunities
are more likely to distribute cash to investors as dividends. Companies with
significant growth opportunities typically retain cash for reinvestment and are,
therefore, less likely to pay a dividend.
Dividends may be regularly scheduled or one-time special dividends. Regular
cash dividends occur when a company pays out a portion of profits on a
consistent schedule (e.g., quarterly). A long-term record of stable or increasing
dividends is widely viewed by investors as a sign of a company’s financial
stability. Companies often choose to maintain a constant dividend per share over
time to avoid adverse signaling.
Special cash dividends (or extraordinary cash dividends) are used when
favorable circumstances allow the firm to make a one-time cash payment to
shareholders, in addition to any regular dividends the firm pays. Many cyclical
firms (e.g., automakers) will use a special dividend to share profits with
shareholders when times are good but maintain the flexibility to conserve cash
when profits are poor.
A company that ceases to operate and has positive net assets may issue a
liquidating dividend. Unlike other dividends, which are distributions of

earnings, a liquidating dividend may be viewed more as a return of capital to
shareholders.
A share repurchase is a transaction in which a company buys outstanding
shares of its own common stock. Share repurchases are an alternative to cash
dividends as a way of distributing cash to shareholders, and they have the same
effect on total shareholders’ wealth as cash dividends of the same size. However,
with a share repurchase, it is up to each shareholder to decide whether to sell
back their shares and receive cash.
A company might repurchase shares to support their price or to signal that
management believes the shares are undervalued. Companies might repurchase
shares to offset an increase in outstanding shares from the exercise of employee
stock options, or to increase reported earnings per share by decreasing the
number of shares outstanding. Companies that want to preserve cash to invest in
growth opportunities when they arise may favor share repurchases over regular
cash dividends. In countries that tax capital gains at lower rates than dividends,
shareholders may prefer share repurchases to dividend payments.
Stock dividends (a.k.a. bonus issues of shares) are dividends paid out in new
shares of stock rather than cash. This results in more shares outstanding, but
each one is worth less, such that total shareholders’ equity remains unchanged.
Stock dividends are commonly expressed as a percentage. A 20% stock dividend
means every shareholder gets 20% more stock.
Stock splits divide each existing share into multiple shares. As with a stock
dividend, this results in more shares, but the price of each share will drop
correspondingly to the number of shares created, so there is no change in the
owner’s wealth or proportional ownership. A stock split that results in more
shares is also known as a forward split, to distinguish it from a reverse stock
split.
Reverse stock splits are the opposite of forward stock splits. After a reverse
split, fewer shares are outstanding, but they have a higher price. Because these
factors offset one another, shareholder wealth is unchanged. Some stock
exchanges require shares to have a minimum price, and a distressed company
whose shares are approaching the minimum price may carry out a reverse stock
split to increase their price and keep its shares listed.
Splits are expressed as a ratio. For example, in a 3-for-1 stock split, each old
share is split into three new shares. In a 1-for-5 reverse stock split, five old

shares become one new share.
Stock splits are currently more common than stock dividends. A company with a
high share price may consider a stock split to make their shares more affordable
for retail investors, increasing liquidity and broadening the shareholder base.
LOS 42.b: Describe dividend payment chronology.
The dates relevant to dividend payments are shown in Figure 42.1.
Figure 42.1: Dividend Payment Chronology
Here is the breakdown:
Declaration date. This is the date that the board of directors approves payment
of a dividend, specifying the per-share dividend amount, the date shareholders
must own the stock to receive the dividend (record date), and the date the
dividend payment will be made (payment date).
Ex-dividend date. This is the first day on which a share purchaser will not
receive the next dividend. The ex-dividend date is one or two business days
before the record date, depending on the settlement period for stock purchases.
If you buy the share on or after the ex-dividend date, you will not receive the
dividend.
Record date. This is the date on which all owners of shares become entitled to
receive the dividend payment on their shares. (The record date for dividends is
different than the record date for proxy voting that we discussed in an earlier
reading.)
Payment date. This is the date that dividend checks are mailed to, or payment
is made electronically to, the shareholders who are entitled to receive the
dividend.
On the ex-dividend date, the share price would decrease from the previous day’s
closing price by the amount of the dividend, in the absence of other market-
related and company-specific factors that affect the stock price.

risk level is the same as that of the overall market, calculate the percentage
change in the share price on the ex-dividend date that is attributable to

MODULE QUIZ 42.1
1. A company is evaluating the likely effects on its share price of declaring a 50% stock
dividend or a 3-for-2 stock split. Other things equal, which of these will result in a lower
share price?
A. A 3-for-2 stock split will result in a lower share price.
B. A 50% stock dividend will result in a lower share price.
C. Both should have the same effect.
2. The first date on which the purchaser of a stock will not receive a dividend that has been
declared is the:
A. declaration date.
B. ex-dividend date.
C. holder-of-record date.
MODULE 42.2: RETURN CALCULATIONS FOR
EQUITIES
LOS 42.c: Calculate price and total return for equity securities.

A rate of return on an equity security that is calculated based only on a price
increase or decrease (adjusted for stock splits) is referred to as its price return.
A rate of return that is calculated based on both price changes and income (i.e.,
cash dividends) is called its total return.
EXAMPLE: Price return and total return
An investor buys Stock Q for $42 and later sells it for $50. The investor
receives a $2 cash dividend just before selling the stock. Calculate the
investor’s price return and total return for the holding period.

EXAMPLE: Effect of a stock split on equity returns
Continuing the previous example, assume the issuer of Stock Q splits the stock
2-for-1 at the same time it pays the cash dividend. Calculate the investor’s
price return and total return for the holding period.

After the stock split, the investor owns two shares that each pay a $1 cash
dividend, so the investor still receives $2. The stock split does not change the
investor’s rate of return. This would also be the case for a stock dividend or a
reverse stock split.
In the previous examples, we assumed the investor received a cash dividend just
before selling the stock. If a cash dividend occurs earlier in the holding period,
an investor can earn additional income by investing the cash received.
Reinvested dividends refer to the investment strategy of using cash dividends to
buy more shares of the same stock. Alternatively, an investor can use cash
dividends to pursue different investments.
If a shareholder receives a cash dividend during the holding period and reinvests

was at the beginning of the period. We can state the additional fractional shares
the investor buys, per share originally owned, as D / PPD, where D is the
dividend per share and PPD is the price per share on the dividend payment date.

MODULE QUIZ 42.2
1. An investor buys Stock E for $85. The stock pays a cash dividend of $3, which the
investor reinvests in Stock E for $84. At the end of the period, the share price of Stock E
is $83. The investor’s holding period return is closest to:
A. −2.4%.
B. 0.0%.
C. 1.1%.
2. Stock W does not pay a cash dividend but declares and pays a 10% stock dividend. For
an investor who owns Stock W, this stock dividend will most likely:
A. increase the investor’s holding period return.
B. decrease the investor’s holding period return.
C. have no effect on the investor’s holding period return.
KEY CONCEPTS
LOS 42.a
Regular cash dividends are paid at set intervals. A special or extraordinary cash
dividend is a one-time cash payment to shareholders.
Stock dividends are additional shares of stock. Stock splits divide each existing
share into multiple shares. In either case, the value of each share will decrease
because the total value of outstanding shares is unchanged. The portion of the
company owned by each shareholder is also unchanged.
In a reverse stock split, the number of shares owned by each shareholder is
decreased, so total shares outstanding are decreased and the value of a single
share is increased.
A share repurchase is a purchase by a company of its outstanding shares. Share
repurchases are an alternative to cash dividends as a way to distribute cash to
shareholders.
LOS 42.b
Dividend payment chronology:
The declaration date is the date that the board of directors approves payment
of the dividend.
The ex-dividend date is the first day that a share of stock trades without the
dividend, one or two business days before the record date. On the ex-dividend
date, the value of each share would decrease by the amount of the dividend, in
the absence of any other factors that affect the share price.

The record date is the date on which share owners who will receive the
dividend are identified.
The payment date is the date that the dividend checks are sent to, or payment is
transferred to, shareholders.
LOS 42.c
Price return is the rate of return on an equity security based only on its price
increase or decrease. Total return is the rate of return based on both price
changes and dividends.
ANSWER KEY FOR MODULE QUIZZES

number of shares by 50%, while neither will affect value of the company.
Therefore, the decrease in the share price should be the same in either case.
(LOS 42.a)
. B The chronology of a dividend payout is declaration date, ex-dividend date,
record date, and payment date. The ex-dividend date is the cutoff date for
receiving the dividend: investors who purchase the stock on or after the ex-
dividend date will not receive the dividend. (LOS 42.b)
